title: How Much Power Do AI Data Centers Actually Need?
description: AI data centers currently consume 288 TWh annually, approximately 6.4% of US grid capacity. Under base case projections, new AI capacity could reach 50 GW by 2030.
content:
The question everyone in energy markets is asking right now has a frustratingly wide answer: somewhere between 35 and 75 gigawatts of new capacity by 2030.

That range matters. At the low end, existing grid infrastructure can probably absorb it with modest upgrades. At the high end, the US needs to build the equivalent of the entire UK electrical grid in five years.

## Where we are today

US data centers consumed approximately 288 TWh of electricity in 2025, representing about 6.4% of total grid capacity. That number was under 3% as recently as 2022. The acceleration is driven almost entirely by AI training and inference workloads.

A single NVIDIA H100 GPU consumes about 700W under load. A modern AI training rack runs 40-80 kW. An AI-optimized data center campus draws 100-500 MW. For context, 500 MW is enough to power a small city.

## The variance drivers

The 35-75 GW range depends on three variables:

**GPU power density**: Blackwell Ultra racks draw 120 kW, nearly double the previous generation. If inference workloads scale as expected, per-rack power demand keeps climbing.

**Hyperscaler capex execution**: The Big Four (Amazon, Google, Meta, Microsoft) committed $328B in combined 2025 capex. If even 60% of that translates to physical facilities, the power demand curve steepens significantly.

**Grid interconnection speed**: The average queue-to-energize timeline is 4+ years in PJM, the largest US electricity market. New generation capacity cannot come online faster than the grid can connect it.

## What this means for investors

The physical constraints are the thesis. You cannot download a power plant. You cannot 3D-print a large power transformer. The companies that build, own, and operate power infrastructure are positioned for a multi-year demand cycle that has no software shortcut.

GridTilt's [Thesis Calculator](/trade) lets you model these scenarios directly. Adjust the assumptions and see how total capex, transformer demand, and nuclear build requirements change across the 35-75 GW range.

## The bottom line

AI data center power demand is not a forecast problem. The facilities are being built right now. The question is whether the power supply chain can keep up. Based on current transformer lead times (4+ years), interconnection queues (4+ years), and nuclear restart timelines (3-5 years), the answer is: probably not without significant bottlenecks.

title: AI Power Infrastructure Stocks: The Complete Guide
description: Overview of 60+ stocks across 8 sectors tied to the AI power infrastructure buildout, from GPU makers to nuclear utilities to construction firms.
content:
The AI power infrastructure thesis spans 8 distinct sectors and over 60 publicly traded companies. This is not a single-stock story. The buildout requires silicon, steel, uranium, copper, concrete, and years of construction.

## The 8 sectors

### Compute
NVIDIA, TSMC, AMD, Micron. The GPU makers and foundries driving AI demand. NVIDIA alone holds 80%+ market share in AI training accelerators. Every GPU sold eventually requires power infrastructure to operate.

### Nuclear Power
Constellation Energy (CEG), Vistra (VST), Talen Energy (TLN), Oklo. Nuclear generators provide the 24/7 baseload power AI data centers need. Microsoft's deal to restart Three Mile Island with Constellation set the precedent. Meta's 6.6 GW nuclear RFP is the largest corporate nuclear procurement in history.

### Uranium and Fuel Cycle
Cameco (CCJ), NexGen Energy (NXE), Uranium Energy Corp (UEC). Every nuclear restart and new build requires enriched uranium fuel. Western uranium supply is constrained, with significant Kazakh import risk.

### Power Hardware
GE Vernova (GEV), Eaton (ETN), Vertiv (VRT). Transformer lead times are 4+ years. Switchgear, PDUs, and cooling systems are backordered across the industry. These companies are the physical supply chain.

### Utilities
NextEra (NEE), Dominion (D), Southern Company (SO). Regulated utilities negotiating long-term power purchase agreements with hyperscalers. Grid interconnection is their bottleneck and their moat.

### Data Center REITs
Equinix (EQIX), Digital Realty (DLR), IREN. The physical facilities where AI compute runs. Occupancy rates above 95% in major markets.

### Construction and EPC
Quanta Services (PWR), EMCOR (EME), MasTec (MTZ). Record backlogs driven by both data center and transmission line construction. These companies physically build the infrastructure.

### ETF Benchmarks
URA, URNM, NLR, GRID, PAVE. ETFs that provide diversified exposure to uranium, nuclear, grid infrastructure, and construction sectors.

title: Nuclear Energy and AI Data Centers: Why It Matters
description: Nuclear power provides the 24/7 baseload electricity AI data centers require. Three Mile Island restart, Meta's 6.6 GW RFP, and SMR development are reshaping the sector.
content:
AI data centers need one thing above all else: reliable, 24/7 power. Solar and wind are intermittent. Natural gas has carbon concerns and price volatility. Nuclear is the only proven source of carbon-free baseload power at scale.

## The baseload argument

An AI training cluster cannot tolerate interruptions. A 100,000-GPU training run costs millions of dollars per day in compute time. If power drops for even seconds, the entire run may need to restart. This makes intermittent renewables unsuitable as the primary power source for large AI facilities.

Nuclear reactors operate at 90%+ capacity factors, running continuously for 18-24 months between refueling outages. No other energy source matches this reliability profile.

## The restart wave

Microsoft's deal with Constellation Energy to restart Three Mile Island Unit 1 (835 MW) set the precedent in 2024. The plant is expected to return to service in 2028, providing dedicated carbon-free power to Azure data centers.

Meta followed with a 6.6 GW nuclear power Request for Proposal, the largest corporate nuclear procurement in history. If fulfilled, this would require restarting multiple retired nuclear plants or securing output from existing facilities.

## Key stocks

**Constellation Energy (CEG)**: Largest nuclear fleet operator in the US with 13 nuclear plants. The TMI restart and potential Meta contract position CEG as the central equity in the nuclear-AI thesis.

**Vistra Corp (VST)**: 41 GW total generation capacity, including the Comanche Peak nuclear facility. Strong merchant power exposure to rising wholesale prices driven by data center demand.

**Cameco (CCJ)**: Largest Western uranium producer. Every nuclear restart requires fuel. Cameco's Cigar Lake mine produces approximately 18 million pounds of U3O8 annually.

**Oklo (OKLO)**: Advanced nuclear startup building 15 MW Aurora microreactors. An NRC design approval would be the first commercial fast spectrum reactor certification in US history.

title: The PJM Interconnection Queue: AI's Biggest Bottleneck
description: PJM's interconnection queue has 4+ year wait times and 250 GW of pending projects. This bottleneck determines how fast AI data center power can come online.
content:
PJM Interconnection manages the largest electricity market in North America, serving 65 million customers across 13 states from Virginia to Illinois. It is also home to Data Center Alley in Northern Virginia, the highest concentration of hyperscaler facilities in the world.

The bottleneck is the interconnection queue.

## What the queue is

Before any new power generation source or large load (like a data center) can connect to the grid, it must go through an interconnection study process. PJM evaluates whether the grid can physically handle the new connection without causing reliability problems.

As of early 2026, PJM's queue contains over 250 GW of pending interconnection requests. The average time from application to energization is 4+ years. Some projects have been waiting 6-7 years.

## Why it matters for AI

Every new data center needs grid power. Every nuclear restart needs grid connection. Every new gas plant needs grid approval. The queue is the single biggest constraint on how fast AI power infrastructure can be built.

PJM's 2025/2026 capacity auction cleared at $270/MW-day, a record price driven by anticipated load growth from data centers outpacing new supply. This price signal tells the market that supply is not keeping up with demand.

## FERC Order 1920

FERC Order 1920 mandates long-range transmission planning for the first time in a decade. Regional utilities must file 20-year expansion plans that account for projected load growth, including AI data centers. The first filing deadline is July 2026.

Strong filings that acknowledge AI data center demand could unlock hundreds of billions in grid infrastructure spending, benefiting transmission builders like Quanta Services (PWR) and EMCOR (EME).

## The investment implication

The queue creates a natural moat for existing power generators. If it takes 4+ years to bring new supply online, companies that already own operating power plants (CEG, VST, NRG) benefit from rising prices without new competition.

title: Where Are AI Data Centers Being Built? A Map
description: GridTilt tracks 48 AI data center facilities across the US. Virginia, Texas, Iowa, and Oregon lead in capacity. See the interactive map.
content:
GridTilt tracks 48 AI data center facilities across the United States. The geographic distribution reveals clear patterns in how hyperscalers choose locations and where grid stress is concentrating.

## The geographic pattern

**Northern Virginia (PJM)**: Data Center Alley remains the largest cluster, with Amazon, Google, Microsoft, and Meta all operating facilities in Loudoun and Prince William counties. Over 70% of US internet traffic passes through this corridor.

**Central Texas (ERCOT)**: Texas has attracted aggressive expansion from xAI (Memphis Colossus), Oracle, and Amazon due to cheap electricity, available land, and minimal permitting barriers. EIA projects ERCOT wholesale prices could rise 79% by 2027 from data center load.

**Iowa and Illinois (MISO)**: Meta and Google operate some of their largest facilities in Iowa, attracted by wind power availability and low land costs. MISO's reserve margins have dropped to 13.4%, the lowest of any major grid region.

**Oregon and Washington (WECC)**: Google's Dalles campus and Amazon's Oregon facilities leverage Pacific Northwest hydroelectric power. These are some of the lowest-cost power locations in the US.

## Capacity distribution

Of the 48 tracked facilities:
- 28 are operational
- 15 are under construction
- 5 are announced/planned

Total tracked capacity exceeds 20 GW, with the largest single facilities reaching 500+ MW.

## Operator strategies

Each hyperscaler has a distinct geographic strategy. [Google](/operator/google) favors renewable-rich locations. [Amazon](/operator/amazon) clusters in established markets. [Meta](/operator/meta) is pursuing nuclear power at scale. [Microsoft](/operator/microsoft) signed the Three Mile Island restart deal.

title: The Transformer Shortage That Could Slow AI
description: The US produces approximately 60 large power transformers per year. AI data center demand could require 80-150+ annually. Lead times exceed 4 years.
content:
There is a physical object that sits between every power plant and every data center. It weighs 200-400 tons, takes 12-18 months to manufacture, and costs $5-15 million. It is called a large power transformer (LPT), and there are not enough of them.

## The math

The US has approximately 2,000 large power transformers in service. Domestic production capacity is roughly 60 units per year. The existing fleet has an average age of 40+ years, meaning replacement demand alone consumes a significant portion of annual production.

Now add AI data centers.

Under GridTilt's base case scenario (50 GW of new AI capacity by 2030), the US would need approximately 80-100 additional LPTs per year. Under the aggressive scenario (75 GW), that number exceeds 150.

The domestic supply chain cannot produce that many. And importing is difficult: LPTs are custom-engineered for specific voltage and capacity requirements, and most global production is concentrated in a handful of factories in South Korea, Germany, and Japan.

## Who benefits

**GE Vernova (GEV)**: Manufactures transformers and grid equipment. Transformer backlog is at record levels with 4+ year lead times.

**Eaton Corporation (ETN)**: Electrical equipment including switchgear and power distribution units. Order intake for datacenter-related products is the key metric in their earnings reports.

**Hubbell (HUBB)**: Utility electrical equipment manufacturer seeing elevated demand from both grid modernization and data center construction.

## The constraint timeline

The transformer shortage is not temporary. Manufacturing capacity cannot be expanded quickly because the factories themselves require specialized tooling, trained workers, and 2-3 years to build. This creates a multi-year window where demand exceeds supply.

title: Uranium Stocks and AI: The Supply Chain Connection
description: Nuclear restarts driven by AI data center demand are creating new uranium fuel requirements. Western supply is constrained with 40% Kazakh import dependency.
content:
Every nuclear reactor consumes enriched uranium fuel. Every nuclear restart creates new demand for that fuel. And AI data centers are driving the largest wave of nuclear procurement in decades.

## The fuel cycle

Uranium goes through a multi-step process before it reaches a reactor:

1. **Mining**: Extracting U3O8 (yellowcake) from the ground
2. **Conversion**: Converting yellowcake to UF6 gas
3. **Enrichment**: Increasing the U-235 concentration from 0.7% to 3-5%
4. **Fabrication**: Manufacturing fuel assemblies for specific reactor designs

Each step has its own supply chain, lead times, and bottleneck potential. The total timeline from mine to reactor is typically 18-24 months.

## Supply constraints

Global uranium production has been below consumption since 2016. The deficit has been filled by inventory drawdowns, recycled material, and underfeeding at enrichment facilities. These secondary sources are depleting.

The US imports approximately 40% of its uranium from Kazakhstan, creating significant geopolitical supply risk. Sanctions, trade restrictions, or Kazakh production disruptions could tighten supply rapidly.

Uranium spot prices reached approximately $92/lb in March 2026, up from $50/lb in 2023. Long-term contract prices, which represent 85% of utility procurement, have also risen substantially.

## Key miners

**Cameco (CCJ)**: Largest Western producer. Cigar Lake mine in Saskatchewan produces 18M lbs/year. Strong utility contracting book with multi-year forward sales.

**NexGen Energy (NXE)**: Developing the Rook I project in Saskatchewan's Athabasca Basin, one of the highest-grade undeveloped uranium deposits globally. Construction approval received in March 2026.

**Uranium Energy Corp (UEC)**: US-focused uranium producer with ISR (in-situ recovery) operations in Wyoming and Texas. Benefits from US-origin uranium procurement preferences.

## The AI connection

Each 1 GW nuclear restart consumes approximately 400,000 lbs of U3O8 over its initial fuel load and 200,000 lbs annually thereafter. If AI-driven nuclear restarts and new builds add 5-10 GW of capacity, that represents 2-4 million additional pounds of annual uranium demand against an already tight market.

title: Behind-the-Meter Power: Why Hyperscalers Are Building Their Own Plants
description: Amazon, Meta, and Microsoft are contracting directly with power generators, bypassing the grid. This behind-the-meter strategy reshapes utility economics.
content:
The grid interconnection queue is 4+ years. Wholesale electricity prices are rising. Renewable intermittency cannot support 24/7 AI training. The hyperscalers have reached a logical conclusion: build your own power.

## What behind-the-meter means

A behind-the-meter (BTM) power arrangement places a generation source directly at or near the point of consumption, bypassing the transmission and distribution grid. The data center connects directly to a dedicated power plant.

This is not new in concept. Industrial facilities have used cogeneration for decades. What is new is the scale: hyperscalers are signing multi-hundred-megawatt BTM agreements that would have been unprecedented five years ago.

## The deals

**Microsoft + Constellation Energy**: The Three Mile Island Unit 1 restart (835 MW) is structured as a 20-year power purchase agreement delivering nuclear baseload directly to Microsoft's data center operations. This is the highest-profile BTM nuclear deal in history.

**Amazon + Talen Energy**: Amazon acquired a data center campus directly adjacent to Talen's Susquehanna nuclear plant in Pennsylvania, with a BTM power arrangement providing up to 960 MW of nuclear power.

**Meta's 6.6 GW RFP**: Meta issued a request for proposals for 6.6 GW of nuclear power capacity, the largest corporate nuclear procurement ever. The winning bids could include both BTM arrangements and traditional PPAs.

**xAI Memphis Colossus**: xAI's initial Memphis facility used on-site gas turbine generators to power 100,000+ GPUs while waiting for grid interconnection, the purest example of BTM power for AI compute.

## What it means for utilities

BTM arrangements partially bypass the regulated utility model. The data center avoids transmission charges, distribution charges, and in some cases, capacity market obligations. This creates regulatory tension.

Utilities like Dominion (D) and PPL (PPL) are responding by creating specialized data center tariffs that attempt to capture some of the value while providing faster interconnection.

## The investor angle

BTM power favors companies that own generation assets near desirable data center locations. Constellation Energy (CEG) and Vistra (VST) are the best-positioned nuclear generators. GE Vernova (GEV) benefits from gas turbine sales for BTM installations.
